content.user_title: Build Rust WebAssembly Modules for the Browser
content.value_statement: Compute-heavy browser workloads can suffer from JavaScript processing costs and frequent data transfers. This skill guides Rust WebAssembly integration and optimization based on measured bottlenecks.
actual_capabilities: Guide Rust target setup, wasm-pack builds, and packaging for browser, bundler, or Node.js targets.
Provide minimal crate configuration, wasm-bindgen exports, and JavaScript initialization examples.
Explain typed-array copying, mutable-slice copy-back, and WASM-owned buffer lifetime requirements.
Recommend profiling, coarse-grained calls, SIMD benchmarking, and worker-based execution.
Identify cross-origin isolation requirements for shared-memory threading.
Guide binary size optimization, streaming compilation setup, panic debugging, and Vite integration choices.
limitations: The skill supplies guidance and examples, not a bundled Rust compiler, generated package, or automated benchmark suite.
Performance improvements depend on workload size, transfer costs, compiler output, and target browser capabilities.
WASM does not execute GPU shaders or handle DOM styling; browser interactions still require JavaScript bindings.
Threading requires deployment support for cross-origin isolation; SIMD needs compatible targets or a fallback build.

use_cases.title: Move browser computation into Rust
use_cases.description: Evaluate and package a measured image-processing or simulation kernel while keeping browser interactions in JavaScript.

use_cases.title: Reuse Rust computation in a web application
use_cases.description: Expose an existing numeric Rust routine through wasm-bindgen and choose the appropriate wasm-pack packaging target.

use_cases.title: Reduce JavaScript and WASM transfer overhead
use_cases.description: Review typed-array transfers, call frequency, worker placement, and SIMD or threading prerequisites before optimizing.

prompt_templates.title: Assess a first WASM workload
prompt_templates.prompt: Use wasm-rust to assess whether my browser task suits WebAssembly: [task]. Explain transfer costs, required tools, and reasons to keep JavaScript.

prompt_templates.title: Create a minimal browser module
prompt_templates.prompt: Use wasm-rust to create a minimal numeric Rust module for [operation]. Include crate configuration, wasm-bindgen exports, wasm-pack commands, and JavaScript initialization.

prompt_templates.title: Review typed-array transfers
prompt_templates.prompt: Use wasm-rust to review my typed-array integration: [implementation]. Identify copies, recommend coarse calls, and define lifetime rules for any WASM-owned buffers.

prompt_templates.title: Plan measured runtime optimization
prompt_templates.prompt: Use wasm-rust to analyze [profile] for [browser targets]. Propose worker placement, SIMD experiments, threading prerequisites, package optimization, and fallbacks. Separate measured facts from hypotheses.

output_examples.input: Should I move many tiny browser calculations into WASM?
output_examples.output: Frequent small calls can cost more in transfers than they save in computation. Profile first, then consider moving the entire loop into Rust.

output_examples.input: Does a mutable Rust byte slice provide zero-copy access to a JavaScript typed array?
output: The wasm-bindgen mutable-slice binding copies input into WASM and copies mutations back when the call returns.
For zero-copy access, keep ownership in WASM and expose a typed-array view with an explicit lifetime contract.
Recreate views after memory growth, and discard them before Rust frees or reallocates the buffer.

output_examples.input: What should I check before enabling shared-memory threads?
output: Check that the deployment supplies the required cross-origin opener and embedder isolation headers.
Use worker-based execution to keep the main thread responsive.
Validate browser support and retain an appropriate fallback when the support contract requires it.

best_practices: Profile representative workloads and measure transfer overhead before selecting or optimizing WASM.
Keep computation calls coarse and define ownership rules for buffers shared through typed-array views.
Keep bindings and tool versions compatible, and verify browser features and deployment headers before enabling advanced execution.
anti_patterns: Move trivial or DOM-heavy tasks into WASM without measuring whether computation outweighs integration costs.
Treat mutable-slice bindings as zero-copy, or retain views after buffer reallocation or memory growth.
Assume SIMD or shared-memory threads work across all browsers and deployments without compatibility checks.

faq.question: Which AI tools can use this skill?
faq.answer: The marketplace lists support for Claude, Codex, and Claude Code. Rust compilation requires a separate local toolchain.

faq.question: Does WebAssembly always run faster than JavaScript?
faq.answer: No. Small tasks and frequent transfers can erase computational gains. Profile the complete workload before choosing WASM.

faq.question: What does wasm-pack generate?
faq.answer: The build produces a WASM module, JavaScript bindings, and TypeScript declarations. The packaging target determines how applications import the output.

faq.question: Are JavaScript typed-array transfers zero-copy?
faq.answer: Standard slice bindings copy data. Zero-copy views require WASM-owned memory and explicit lifetime rules, including view recreation after memory growth.

faq.question: What do shared-memory threads require?
faq.answer: They require compatible tooling and browser support, plus cross-origin isolation headers. Verify the deployment before relying on threaded execution.

faq.question: Can this skill implement GPU rendering or DOM styling?
faq.answer: Those tasks are outside its scope. WASM targets CPU computation; GPU pipelines need WebGPU tooling, and DOM work uses JavaScript or browser bindings.
